Lessons.Title: Equivalent Equations
ExplanationParagraphs: Learning objective: decide whether equations have the same solution sets, explain operations that preserve equivalence and use contextual interpretation to check. Edulytiks first-party source-aligned lesson based on Illustrative Mathematics Algebra 1 First Edition Unit 2 Lesson 6, https://im.kendallhunt.com/HS/teachers/1/2/6/preparation.html (CC BY 4.0). Building On 6.EE.A.4; Addressing HSA-CED.A.2, HSA-REI.A.1, HSA-SSE.A.1; Building Towards HSA-REI.A.

Equations 3x+9=24, 3x=15 and x=5 are equivalent: each has exactly the solution set {5}. Subtracting 9 from both sides, combining like terms, and multiplying both sides by a nonzero constant preserve the solution set. By contrast, multiplying by zero or dividing by a variable expression that could equal zero can lose information.

Original age context: the older sibling is six years older than the younger, y. Set o=y+6. Equivalent statements o−y=6, 2o−2y=12 hold for the same ordered pairs. They express a relationship rather than one fixed numeric answer. Age constraints o,y≥0 matter even when all algebraic pairs solve.

Student tasks: explain each transformation to a partner, generate two distinct equivalent forms of a contextual equation, test plausible wrong and correct moves, then interpret both equations in words. Teacher-scored rubric (0–2 each, total 8): exact solution-set comparison, valid move justification, correct contextual variable relation, and critique of a non-equivalent transformation.

KeyConcepts.Title: Equivalent equations
KeyConcepts.Definition: Two equations are equivalent if they have exactly the same solutions.
KeyConcepts.Rule: Compare all solutions, not just one shared solution.

KeyConcepts.Title: Valid transformations
KeyConcepts.Definition: Adding the same value, or multiplying by a fixed nonzero constant, on both sides preserves equality solutions.
KeyConcepts.Rule: Never multiply by zero or divide by possibly zero expression without domain analysis.

KeyConcepts.Title: Relational equivalence
KeyConcepts.Definition: Two-variable equations can represent the same relationship in different forms.

WorkedExamples.Title: Transform without changing solutions
WorkedExamples.Question: Show 3x+9=24 is equivalent to x=5.
WorkedExamples.Method: Explain the equivalence or contextual calculation and verify substitutions independently.
Steps: Divide both sides by nonzero 3: x=5.
Reverse: multiply x=5 by 3 to get 3x=15 and add 9 to recover 3x+9=24.
Both equations share exactly one solution.

WorkedExamples.Title: Rearrange a relational equation
WorkedExamples.Question: Are o=y+6 and 2o−2y=12 equivalent over real o,y?
WorkedExamples.Method: Explain the equivalence or contextual calculation and verify substitutions independently.
Steps: From o=y+6, subtract y to obtain o−y=6.
Multiply both sides by nonzero 2 to get 2o−2y=12.
Reverse by dividing by 2 and adding y.
The same ordered pairs satisfy both.
WorkedExamples.Check: Try y=10,o=16; both yield true equalities.

WorkedExamples.Title: Spot lost information
WorkedExamples.Question: Compare x=5 and 0x=0.
WorkedExamples.Method: Explain the equivalence or contextual calculation and verify substitutions independently.
Steps: The first equation requires exactly x=5.
Multiplying both sides of x=5 by zero gives 0x=0.
The second equality is true for every real x, not only 5.
Thus multiplication by zero is not an equivalence-preserving move.
WorkedExamples.Answer: Not equivalent: {5} differs from all real numbers.
WorkedExamples.Check: At x=4, 0x=0 true but x=5 false.

CommonMistakes.Mistake: Treating one shared solution as proof of equivalence
CommonMistakes.WhyWrong: The equations might have other different solutions.

CommonMistakes.Mistake: Dividing by a zero or possibly zero factor
CommonMistakes.WhyWrong: Division is undefined or can eliminate solutions.
CommonMistakes.Correction: State nonzero requirement and check all original solutions.

SummaryPoints: Equivalent equations must have identical solution sets.
Adding or subtracting the same amount and multiplying by a fixed nonzero constant preserve equivalence.
Contextual relationships may have infinitely many ordered-pair solutions.
Teacher-reviewed move explanations are essential; a solved number alone is not sufficient.
